strengths: Novel problem formulation: the paper appears to be the first to study non-smooth submodular-concave min-max/max-min problems (submodular in the set variable, concave in the continuous variable) in both offline and online regimes, filling a genuine gap relative to Adibi et al. (2022) (convex-submodular) and Mualem et al. (2024).

Technically sound and reasonably complete theoretical framework: it combines the subgradient of the Lovász extension for the x-update with a Gaussian-smoothed zeroth-order oracle for the y-update inside an extragradient scheme, and derives expected guarantees for the offline ε-saddle point (O(nm²ε⁻²) queries, Theorem 3.2) and the online duality gap (O(√(N P̄_N)), Theorem 3.6). The bounds I checked (variance bound E||g_μy||² ≤ L_0y²(m+4)², the (h₂/2+h₁) bias term, and the resulting N = O(m²/ε²)) are internally consistent.

Careful treatment of the saddle-point existence issue: Propositions 2.10 and 2.11 and the explicit counterexample/positive example in Appendix B make the assumptions transparent rather than hiding them, and the use of E_τ[f(S_τ,y)] = f^L(x,y) to translate the continuous gap back to the combinatorial gap is clean.

Thorough supplementary material: full proofs, several synthetic numerical studies (adversarial image segmentation, adversarial semi-supervised clustering), and explicit hyperparameters aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is largely incremental: every component (Lovász subgradient, Nesterov-Spokoiny Gaussian smoothing, extragradient/Korpelevich analysis, Zinkevich-style path-length dynamic regret) is standard, and the paper does not introduce a fundamentally new proof technique or estimator.

The central guarantee rests on a strong assumption that a saddle point of the discrete f exists (condition (10)); the paper itself shows this can fail (Appendix B) and only gives sufficient conditions. This substantially limits the reach of the results, and the assumption is not restated in the theorem statements (e.g., Theorem 3.2) where it is actually needed.

The empirical evidence does not convincingly support the headline claims. The U-Net baselines in Table 1 are trained and evaluated without adversaries while Algorithm 1 is evaluated under adversarial perturbation, so the 'outperforms both supervised and semi-supervised U-Nets' claim is not apples-to-apples. The tasks are small and synthetic (50×50 two-segment images, two-moons clustering), and no comparison is made against existing methods for related min-max/submodular problems.

Presentation problems: Algorithm 1 line 6 erroneously writes g_{μy}(z_k) = (1/t_k)Σ g^i_{μy}(ẑ_k) using ẑ_k instead of z_k; the notation in (11) introduces B but immediately fixes B = I; reference handling is inconsistent (e.g., 'Farzin et al., 2024' vs 'Farzin et al., 2025a'); and the exposition is dense with some undefined symbols.

The online step sizes are set using the path length P̄_N, which is not known in advance and is not addressed (no doubling/adaptive scheme), so the stated bound is not directly implementable as written.

Limitations are only partially discussed: sensitivity to the rate of change of the cost functions is mentioned in Appendix E.2, but there is no discussion of the practical cost of the O(nm²ε⁻²) query complexity or of when the saddle-point assumption is realistically satisfied in the motivating applications.

strengths: Addresses an understudied problem class—non-smooth, submodular-concave min-max/max-min problems—in both offline and online regimes, and is to my knowledge the first to combine Lovász-extension subgradients for the minimizer with Gaussian-smoothing zeroth-order oracles for the maximizer within an extragradient scheme.

The theoretical framework is coherent: offline convergence to an ε-saddle point with explicit O(nm²ε⁻²) query complexity, and an online dynamic-regret bound of O(√(N P̄_N)) that correctly mirrors standard path-length results (Zinkevich, 2003).

The paper responsibly discusses when the continuous relaxation (7) is equivalent to the discrete problem (1), providing Proposition 2.10 and sufficient conditions in Proposition 2.11, rather than silently assuming equivalence.

Appendices add useful material: relaxation of the 'four queries per function change' assumption to three (Remarks D.1–D.4), and discussion of backward/central-difference oracles, showing awareness of practical constraints.
weaknesses: Presentation quality is poor and undermines confidence in the technical core. Examples: 'Costum ZO optimiser' in Table 1; the tautological inequality 'E[||G(z_k)||²] ≤ E[||G(z_k)||²]' in the proof of Theorem 3.2; the symbol L (rather than L_0) appearing in the hyperparameter choices of Theorem 3.2; inconsistent notation h_{1,k} vs h_{1k}; Algorithm 1 line 6 references ẑ_k before ẑ_k is produced on line 10; and garbled statements such as the two lines of Eq. (30) which are written identically.

Experimental evidence is far too weak to support the paper's claims. All experiments are toy/synthetic: 50×50 two-segment grayscale images and two-moons datasets with 40–50 points. This is insufficient to demonstrate that the method 'solves' the general problem class.

The comparison to U-Net in Table 1 is not an apples-to-apples evaluation and the conclusion is overclaimed. The U-Nets are trained on a base image with rotations/translations and evaluated on a video with different trajectories; the claim that Algorithm 1 'outperforms' supervised/semi-supervised U-Nets is misleading (e.g., its recall 0.989 is actually lower than supervised U-Net's 0.994).

The central saddle-point-existence condition, Eq. (10), is assumed rather than verified for any of the application examples (adversarial segmentation, adversarial clustering). Since Proposition 2.10 shows a saddle point need not exist in general, the theory may not apply to the very examples used to illustrate it.

Theoretical novelty is incremental. The method is a combination of existing building blocks (extragradient, Nesterov–Spokoiny Gaussian smoothing, Hazan–Kale Lovász subgradients) and the rates obtained are the standard ones for nonsmooth convex-concave problems; no new insight or improved guarantee is provided.

Reproducibility is limited: no code is released, several hyperparameters are only partially specified, and the 'real-time 60 fps' claim is demonstrated only on the toy 50×50 video. Strong statements such as 'no choice of algorithmic parameters yields a correct segmentation' for ρ < 5 are asserted without rigorous justification.

The bias term μL_{0y}m^{1/2} is constant in N and is only removed by an assumption on μ tied to the target ε; combined with the (m+4)² factor from the Gaussian oracle variance, this drives the m² dependence in the offline complexity, which is not discussed critically.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: to the best of my knowledge this is the first study of offline and online min-max/max-min problems with non-smooth submodular-concave objectives, combining the Lovász-extension subgradient (for the set player) with Gaussian-smoothed zeroth-order oracles (for the continuous player) inside an extragradient framework.

The theoretical treatment is fairly comprehensive: Theorem 3.2 gives an expectation bound on the restricted gap and duality gap of the Lovász extension with explicit hyperparameter choices yielding an ε-saddle point in O(nm²ε⁻²) value-oracle calls, and Theorem 3.6 gives an O(√(N P̄_N)) online duality gap that correctly reduces to the classical dynamic-regret form. I checked the algebra of the online step sizes (h₂ ∝ √(ē₀²+3D_z P̄_N)/(√(L²+L₀y²(m+4)²)√(N+1))) and the terms do combine to O(√(N P̄_N)) as claimed.

The paper carefully handles a subtle but important issue — that a discrete saddle point need not exist — via Propositions 2.10 and 2.11, giving explicit sufficient conditions under which solving the continuous relaxation (7) recovers a solution of the combinatorial problem (1). Appendix B provides concrete illustrative examples.

Interesting and relevant applications (adversarial semi-supervised image segmentation and clustering), with real-time performance and low memory footprint, and an honest discussion of the robustness-accuracy trade-off as a function of the adversarial budget ρ.
Limitations are treated honestly (Appendix D.3/D.4 on the three-query relaxation, sensitivity to the rate of change of the cost, and the non-vanishing O(NV) error term when the estimator is biased).
weaknesses: Algorithm 1 contains a concrete error: line 6 defines g_{μ_y}(z_k) as the average of g^i_{μ_y}(ẑ_k), but it should be evaluated at z_k (the forward step). Similarly the sequence of sampled directions u_k should be tied to the forward point, not the lookahead point. This makes the pseudocode as written inconsistent with the analysis.

Presentation issues throughout: typographical errors ('extragrdient', 'Costum ZO optimiser'), inconsistent British/American spelling ('minimiser'/'minimizer'), Definition 2.2 uses both \tilde{S} and \bar{S}, and several equations (e.g., the statement of Lemma 2.7, the min-max objective in Proposition 2.11) are garbled. These are fixable but numerous.

The online guarantee rests on the strong modeling assumption that the cost function is fixed long enough for at least four (or three) function queries per round. This 'piecewise-stationary' assumption restricts the online result relative to a fully adversarial sequence, and the relaxed version (Remark D.4) only yields a non-vanishing O(NV) extra error.

There is a modeling ambiguity in the online regret: the decision maker is said to play (S_k, y_k) before observing f_k, yet the regret is measured on the lookahead point ẑ_k which is computed using f_k. Unless one adopts the 'fixed function within a round' interpretation, this would give the regret access to information not available at play time; the paper does not explicitly reconcile these two readings.

Empirical evaluation is thin and arguably unfair: all experiments are on synthetic data, and the headline comparison pits the algorithm against U-Nets that are trained and evaluated without adversaries on a narrow training distribution. This stacks the deck in favor of the proposed method, and no comparison is made against other min-max or submodular-optimization baselines. The practical examples also never verify that condition (10) (existence of a discrete saddle point / vertex minimizer) actually holds, which is required for the relaxation to be valid.

The dimension dependence O(m²) in the offline rate is high (though standard for two-point ZO estimators); the paper does not discuss whether this is improvable (e.g., via coordinate-wise or one-point estimators) or how it compares to first-order alternatives when the y-gradient is available.

strengths: The paper tackles a novel and challenging problem: non-smooth submodular-concave min-max optimization in offline and online settings, combining Lovász extension subgradients with Gaussian smoothing and extragradient.

It provides convergence rate O(n m^2 ε^{-2}) for the offline continuous problem and an online dynamic regret bound O(sqrt(N(1+\bar P))), extending zeroth-order min-max methods to submodular structures.
The algorithm is derivative-free and only requires function evaluations, which is suitable for non-smooth settings.
The paper includes numerical experiments on adversarial image segmentation and semi-supervised clustering, demonstrating practical potential.
The theoretical analysis is mostly clear and the proofs for the continuous Lovász extension problem appear technically sound.
weaknesses: The main theoretical guarantee is for the continuous Lovász extension, not the original discrete min-max problem. The rounding step (sampling τ) only ensures max_y E_τ[f(S,y)] - min_S f(S,y) ≤ ε, whereas an ε-saddle point requires max_y f(S,y) - min_S f(S,y) ≤ ε. Since max_y E_τ[f(S,y)] ≤ E_τ[max_y f(S,y)], the bound does not imply the claimed discrete guarantee. This is a fundamental gap in the central claim.

The online bound similarly controls sum max_y E_τ[f_k(S_k,y)] - min_S f_k(S,y_k), which is weaker than the expected online duality gap E[sum max_y f_k(S_k,y) - min_S f_k(S,y_k)]. The paper does not address this discrepancy.

The online setting assumes enough time for at least four function queries between function changes, but Algorithm 1 requires O(n) function evaluations per iteration (e.g., 6n). This assumption is unrealistic and not justified for large n.

The empirical comparison to U-Net is unfair: Algorithm 1 is evaluated under adversarial perturbations while U-Nets are not, and the U-Nets are trained on a small synthetic dataset without tuning. The claim that Algorithm 1 outperforms U-Nets is not well supported.

The numerical validation is weak: no duality gap or convergence rate plots, no comparison to other min-max submodular methods, and limited reproducibility details (e.g., U-Net training, seeds, error bars).
Some presentation issues: typo in equation (30), inconsistent notation (u vs y for adversary), and unclear definition of D_τ.
The paper assumes the existence of a saddle point and conditions (10) but does not verify them in experiments, limiting applicability.
The online bound depends on a known path-length bound \bar P; if \bar P grows linearly with N, the bound becomes vacuous, and the paper does not discuss how to obtain \bar P in practice.
The limitations discussion does not acknowledge the discrete rounding gap or the unrealistic online query assumption.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and relatively under-explored problem: min-max/max-min optimization where the objective is submodular in the combinatorial (set) variable and concave, possibly non-smooth, in the continuous variable, in both offline and online regimes.

Provides explicit convergence guarantees and complexity analysis: an expected epsilon-saddle point for the offline case with O(n m^2 epsilon^{-2}) function queries, and an online duality gap of order O(sqrt(N(1+P_bar))) with hyperparameter selection rules; the online path-length (dynamic regret) analysis and the discussion of relaxing the per-iteration query budget (Remarks D.3/D.4) are non-trivial technical extensions.

The algorithmic idea — using the exact Lovász-extension subgradient for the set variable (obtainable from value queries only) together with a Gaussian-smoothed zeroth-order oracle for the continuous variable inside an extragradient loop — is clean and internally consistent, and the per-iteration cost argument (Remark 3.3) is reasonable.
Numerical illustrations on adversarial semi-supervised image segmentation and semi-supervised clustering show the method can track solutions in synthetic, resource-constrained, online settings.
weaknesses: The whole method is justified only under strong and hard-to-verify assumptions. Saddle-point existence for f and the equivalence between the continuous relaxation (7) and the discrete problem (1) rest on Proposition 2.11, whose conditions (zeta being a Lovász extension, minimizer sets containing a vertex, or a common vertex minimizer) are restrictive. The numerical experiments never check these conditions, so it is unclear whether the method actually solves (1) on the reported applications rather than merely (7).

The empirical comparison is weak and arguably unfair. Table 1 compares the proposed optimizer (which uses seeds and is run under adversarial perturbation) against U-Nets that are trained and evaluated without adversaries and take different inputs; listing 'Theoretical Guarantees: Yes' as a table row is not a performance metric. Metrics are also computed inconsistently (the first 120 frames are discarded only for the proposed method). Data are synthetic two-segment images / two-moon clusters, which do not stress-test the claims.

Novelty is incremental: the contribution is essentially a combination of existing components (Lovász subgradient for submodular minimization, Nesterov–Spokoiny Gaussian smoothing, extragradient), and no fundamentally new insight or technique is introduced.

The 'first study' claim and the dismissal of the closest related work (Adibi et al., 2022, convex-submodular minimax) as 'not sensible' to compare are not adequately justified, making it difficult to situate the contribution relative to prior art.

Presentation problems that hinder reproducibility: notation collisions (S used both for the seed set and the set variable of (1)), an undefined symbol (the deterministic path-length bound is written as tilde P in the text but as P_bar elsewhere), an inconsistency in Algorithm 1 (line 6 averages g_{mu_y}^i(z_hat_k) rather than at z_k), and a malformed reference list.
No code/reproducibility statement is provided, and hyperparameters (h1, h2, mu, rho, lambda, t_k) appear tuned per experiment, which limits confidence in the empirical results.

strengths: The paper addresses a novel and well-motivated problem: min-max/max-min optimization with non-smooth submodular-concave objectives, which has not been systematically studied before.

The proposed algorithm creatively combines the Lovász extension subgradient for the discrete minimizer with Gaussian smoothing and an extragradient scheme for the continuous maximizer, requiring only zeroth-order information.

The theoretical analysis covers both offline and online settings, providing convergence rates (O(nm^2 ε^-2) function queries offline and O(√(N(1+\bar P))) online path-length-dependent bound) with detailed proofs in the appendix.
The numerical experiments on adversarial image segmentation and semi-supervised clustering demonstrate the method's practical potential, including real-time operation and robustness.
The paper includes a thoughtful discussion of limitations and future directions, such as extending to weakly submodular functions and unbounded sets.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is not fully supported. The theorems bound the duality gap of the Lovász extension f^L, e.g., max_y f^L(x,y) - min_x f^L(x,y), where f^L(x,y)=E_τ f(S_τ,y). However, an ε-saddle point of the original function f requires max_y f(S,y) - min_S f(S,y) ≤ ε. Since max_y E_τ f(S_τ,y) ≤ E_τ max_y f(S_τ,y), bounding the former does not imply a bound on the latter. Thus, the paper does not establish the claimed ε-saddle point guarantee for f. The same issue appears in the online setting: Definition 3.4 requires sum max_y f_k(S_k,y) - min_S f_k(S,y_k), but Theorem 3.6 bounds a weaker quantity involving max_y E_τ. This undermines the main contributions.
Algorithm 1 contains a pseudocode error: line 6 computes g_{\mu_y}(z_k) using \hat{z}_k before \hat{z}_k is defined; it should use z_k. This harms reproducibility and clarity.

The theorems state that constant step sizes are used, but the recommended hyperparameters depend on N (e.g., h_2 ∝ 1/√N). The theory also assumes t_k=1, while experiments use t=10–20 without a corresponding theoretical justification.

The numerical comparison to U-Net is not apples-to-apples: the U-Nets are trained and evaluated without adversaries, while Algorithm 1 operates under adversarial perturbations. The claim that Algorithm 1 outperforms U-Nets is therefore overstated. No code or detailed runtime/memory measurements are provided.

The presentation has numerous typos, inconsistent notation (e.g., \mathcal{Y} vs \mathcal{V}), broken or duplicate references, and confusing definitions (e.g., D_τ). These issues reduce readability and make some arguments hard to follow.
